objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why each before-takeoff item is checked and what a bad reading means, position the airplane well for the run-up, review takeoff performance and brief the takeoff, and teach a learner to do all of it while dividing attention, handling runway changes and wake turbulence, and planning for an engine failure, as you spot and fix the errors learners make.
why: The before-takeoff check is the last good chance to find a problem on the ground, and the AIH calls the moment just before takeoff the second easiest point in a flight to make a critical safety decision [[25:20|AIH 1-16]]. About twenty percent of general aviation accidents happen during takeoff and departure climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Your learners will run up the way you taught them for the rest of their flying lives, so the habit you build now is the one that catches the bad magneto years later [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

prereading.what: The before-takeoff check: oil temperature, choosing and setting up the run-up spot, dividing attention, the systems list, the sample takeoff briefing and the takeoff checks.
prereading.label: AFH 2-21 to 2-22

prereading.what: What to do before takeoff, the rejected takeoff, engine failure after liftoff and the turn-back analysis.
prereading.label: AFH 6-1 to 18-8

prereading.what: What the mixture, carburetor heat, magneto and ammeter checks show; takeoff performance factors; runway incursions, runway confusion and ATC instructions.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-9 to 14-35

prereading.what: Overlearned checklists, attention switching and interruptions, learning from errors, primacy, the sterile flight deck, and managing risk while teaching takeoffs.
prereading.label: AIH 3-28 to 10-8

prereading.what: Run-up trouble as a powerplant hazard, takeoff performance and environment hazards, and a fatal turf-runway takeoff case study.
prereading.label: RMH 3-4 to C-2

prereading.what: Vortex avoidance when departing, and the wake turbulence intervals ATC applies to departures.
prereading.label: AIM 7-4-6 to 7-4-9

warmup: Think first: your learner has done fifteen run-ups and recites the checklist perfectly. Today you ask, "Why do we check each magneto by itself?" and she answers, "Because the checklist says so." Is that a problem if she never misses an item? What would you change about her next run-up, and what would you want her to say instead?

key_terms.def: The systematic AFM/POH procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments and avionics before flight, normally done at a run-up position near the takeoff end of the runway.
Running the engine at the power the POH gives for the engine checks, with the brakes holding the airplane still.
A small chip or nick in a propeller leading edge that concentrates stress and can grow into a crack and blade failure.
Moving the ignition switch from BOTH to RIGHT and from BOTH to LEFT and watching the rpm drop; the allowed drop is in the AFM/POH.
Moving a constant-speed propeller control through a full cycle during the run-up to prove the system works and to bring warm oil into the governor.
A short spoken plan given out loud before takeoff: type of takeoff, runway, wind, rotation speed, initial heading and altitude, and what the pilot will do if the engine fails.
The POH takeoff ground roll plus landing ground roll, a good estimate of the runway needed to reach takeoff speed and then stop.
Moving attention back and forth between tasks, such as a checklist and the view outside; a deferred task is easy to forget.
An unexpected event for which the learner stops one task to do another, a common cause of skipped checklist steps.
A takeoff that begins at a taxiway intersection instead of the runway end, leaving less runway; the pilot decides if it is long enough.
Where a departing aircraft lifts its nose; its wake begins there, so a following airplane rotates before that point.
Following the clearance you expected instead of the one you received, a known pitfall of pretaxi planning.

chunks.title: What the run-up is for, and what you are really teaching

body.p: The before-takeoff check is the systematic AFM/POH procedure for checking the engine, controls, systems, instruments and avionics before flight. It is normally done after taxiing to a run-up position near the takeoff end of the runway [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. All run-up and pretakeoff checklist items should be finished before taxiing onto the runway [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
The ACS asks you to explain the purpose of the checklist items (K1) in three parts. Teach each one by name so the learner knows why the card exists, not just what is on it.

head: ACS purpose
What it means in the airplane
Source
rows: Every line has a job: fuel set to the right tank, trim set for takeoff, controls free through their whole range, engine and systems in limits, instruments and avionics set, and a spoken takeoff plan.
The run-up is a test. A magneto drop over the limit, a full-scale ammeter, low suction or an altimeter that is far off are failures found on the ground instead of in the climb.
Ensuring the aircraft is in safe operating condition as recommended by the manufacturer (K1c)
The AFM/POH checklist and its limits decide what is acceptable, and the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence over the handbooks.

body.p: It is also a decision point. The second easiest point in a flight to make a critical safety decision is just before takeoff, and the 5P check there helps the pilot make a reasoned go/no-go decision [[25:20|AIH 1-16]].

Your real job is the habit. A checklist is a memory aid with the emphasis on the "check", and it has no value if the pilot is not committed to using it. Establishing habit patterns is a major objective of primary training, and the instructor should promote a positive attitude toward checklist use [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. Before each flight, discuss safety and the use of the checklist, because learners learn by watching you [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. By the principle of primacy, make sure the learner gets it right the first time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: The ACS is a testing tool, not a teaching tool [[25:171|AIH 9-1]]. Teach why each item matters; passing the check ride follows from that.

check.q: Why does the AIH treat the moment before takeoff as more than a systems check?
check.a: It is one of the two critical go/no-go points of every flight, the second easiest place to make a critical safety decision, and the 5P check there supports a reasoned decision [[25:20|AIH 1-16]].

body.p: Reasons for checking each item (K1a) is where most learners are weakest. They know the words on the card but not what each one protects against. Teach every item as a pair: what you check, and why.

head: Item
What you check and why
Source
rows: Many engines need a minimum oil temperature from the AFM/POH before takeoff power is applied. Verify it is in range before any high power.
Set per the AFM/POH, verified ON, with the proper tank selected.
Set for takeoff; elevator trim, and on some airplanes rudder and aileron trim too.
Full aileron, elevator and rudder deflection in all directions. Moving them only part way is common and not acceptable.
Temperatures and pressures normal, magnetos or FADEC within limits, carburetor heat working, and a constant-speed propeller operating as the engine keeps running normally.
Voltage within range and the battery shown charging.
An acceptable vacuum, and enough time for mechanical gyros to spin up. A hasty taxi and run-up makes a departure into IMC unadvisable.
Rechecked and set; heading indicator agrees with the magnetic compass; heading bug on the runway or assigned heading.
Frequencies, initial navigation sources and courses, autopilot preselects and the transponder code.
Said out loud even when alone, including a visual check of the correct surface and direction.

body.p: Why bother with the why? A learner who understands a process masters variations of it more easily, such as unfamiliar aircraft and new avionics [[25:61|AIH 3-10]]. The opposite is overlearning: a verbal checklist can become so automatic that the recitation is decoupled from the thoughts and actions it should trigger [[25:79|AIH 3-28]].

callout.text: Application: for every item, ask three questions. What am I checking? What would a bad reading look like? What would I do about it?

check.q: Your learner moves the yoke about halfway each way and calls "controls free and correct." What do you teach?
check.a: The check is full deflection of aileron, elevator and rudder in all directions; partial movement is a common error and not acceptable [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

chunks.title: Detecting malfunctions: what each check tells you

body.p: Detecting malfunctions (K1b) means reading each check like a test result. Teach the normal answer and the bad answers before the learner ever sees one, so a bad reading is recognized and not explained away.

head: Check
Normal
Malfunction
Source
rows: A small rpm drop on each magneto, within the AFM/POH limit

The engine stops on one magneto or the drop exceeds the limit: do not fly until it is corrected. Causes include fouled plugs, broken or shorted wires and improper timing. No drop at all is also not normal.
The rpm drops and then stays constant
The rpm drops, then slowly rises as ice melts: ice was present.
Manifold pressure drops, then slowly rises: ice was present.
Cycled through a full cycle and back; proves the system works and brings warm oil into the governor
Skipping it risks an engine overspeed on takeoff.
Plus side shows the battery charging
Full-scale minus: alternator or generator malfunction. Full-scale plus: regulator malfunction. Consult the AFM/POH.
Low suction: the attitude and heading indicators may not give reliable information.
Within 75 feet of field elevation with the current setting
More than 75 feet off: accuracy questionable; refer it to a repair station.
Heading within 5 degrees of the runway when aligned; horizon bar stays level in straight taxi
Horizon bar tips more than 5 degrees in taxi turns: unreliable.
Smooth after leaning per the AFM/POH
Roughness at run-up power from too rich a mixture, which fouls plugs.

body.p: Teach that run-up trouble is a real hazard, not a nuisance. The RMH lists difficulty with an engine run-up, or an engine issue after maintenance, as a possible significant powerplant hazard [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. The AIH opens with a learner and instructor whose runaway engine, the day after an annual, came from a throttle rod-end with no bolt or nut [[25:5|AIH 1-1]].

callout.text: Watch for the learner who rechecks a bad magneto until it looks better and then calls it good. The PHAK rule is simple: over the limit or the engine quits, do not fly until the problem is corrected [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

check.q: The ammeter swings to full-scale plus at run-up rpm. Your learner says, "Great, it's charging hard." What do you teach?
check.a: A full-scale positive deflection indicates a regulator malfunction; consult the AFM/POH for the action to take [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

chunks.title: Safe operating condition as the manufacturer recommends

body.p: Ensuring the aircraft is in safe operating condition as recommended by the manufacturer (K1c) means the AFM/POH, not memory or a generic card, sets the standard. Each airplane has different features and equipment, so its own before-takeoff checklist is used for the run-up [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Where the AFH and the manufacturer differ, the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

bullets: The permissible magneto drop is listed in the AFM or POH [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].
Oil pressure limits come from the AFM/POH; green is normal and red marks the minimum and maximum [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]].
Vacuum values and cowl flap settings come from the AFM/POH [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
The AFM/POH is required aboard and is essential for resolving equipment malfunctions [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].
Personal checklists are fine when built from the manufacturer's checklist, with additions for the specific aircraft and operation [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

body.p: Instructor angle. Determine the aircraft's official airworthiness status before scheduled flights, know how the operator reports discrepancies, and review the current discrepancy report; consider involving the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. The PIC is directly responsible for, and the final authority on, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]], so teach the learner that the no-go call after a failed check is theirs to make.

callout.text: Sources differ on vacuum. The AFH says typically 4.8 to 5.2 "Hg at 2,000 rpm [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]; the PHAK says usually 4.5 to 5.5 "Hg [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Teach the POH number for the airplane you fly.

check.q: A transfer learner brings a laminated generic run-up card from another school to your airplane. What do you tell him?
check.a: Use this airplane's AFM/POH checklist, because each airplane has different features and equipment [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]; a personal checklist is fine only if it is built from the manufacturer's checklist [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

chunks.title: Position the airplane: wind, prop blast and debris

body.p: Where the learner stops matters before any item on the card. A run-up spot should be firm, a smooth paved or turf surface if possible, and free of debris. Otherwise the propeller can pick up pebbles, dirt, mud or sand and hurl them backward, damaging the propeller and possibly the tail. Small chips in a propeller leading edge form stress risers that may lead to cracks and blade failure [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

head: ACS S3 factor
What to teach
Source
rows: Head the airplane as nearly as possible into the wind. Tightly cowled air-cooled engines get little cooling air on the ground and can overheat cylinders before oil temperature rises; watch cylinder head temperature if installed and set cowl flaps per the AFM/POH.
Stop clear of other aircraft and of the taxiway, and keep other aircraft out of the propeller wash.
Nothing behind the airplane that the propeller blast could damage; no personnel or ground equipment in the propeller wash.
Applies to seaplanes, not ASEL; a passing remark is enough for this course.

body.p: Then align the nosewheel. After positioning, let the airplane roll forward slightly so the nosewheel or tailwheel lines up with the longitudinal axis [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]. Stopping with the nosewheel straight also relieves side load and makes it easier to move ahead [[24:57|AFH 2-20]].

callout.text: Application: before the learner adds run-up power, have her say out loud what is behind the tail and which way the wind is blowing. It costs five seconds and builds the S3 habit.

check.q: Your learner stops on a gravel patch, nose downwind, with an open hangar behind the tail. Name three problems.
check.a: Gravel can be thrown into the propeller and tail, causing stress risers; the blast can damage what is behind; and a downwind run-up gives poor engine cooling [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

chunks.title: Verify engine parameters and airplane configuration

body.p: S5 has two halves: the engine is healthy and the airplane is set up for this takeoff. As a minimum before every takeoff, all engine instruments are checked for proper indications and all controls for full, free and correct movement [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

bullets: Configuration first: as many items as possible, such as flaps, trim and GPS inputs, are set before initial taxi [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]], then confirmed on the before-takeoff checklist.
Gyros need time: allow about 5 minutes after start for the heading indicator to spin up [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
Before the roll, runway numbers on a paved runway should agree with the magnetic compass and heading indicator [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: The last check as power comes up to full takeoff power covers six questions [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]:

bullets: Doors latched and windows closed as required?
Controls positioned for any crosswind?
Power correct?
Engine rpm normal?
Engine smooth?
Engine instruments normal and in the green?

body.p: With a constant-speed propeller, the tachometer should come up to within 40 rpm of the red line as soon as full power is applied and stay there for the takeoff [[24:239|AFH 12-8]]. A fixed-pitch propeller reaches full rpm only as the airplane accelerates [[24:239|AFH 12-8]], so teach the learner the POH static rpm for your trainer.

callout.text: Failure to check engine instruments for signs of malfunction after applying takeoff power is an AFH common error [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]. Teach one deliberate glance at the gauges, called out loud, early in the roll.

check.q: On the takeoff roll your learner's eyes never leave the centerline. Which AFH common error is that, and what do you coach?
check.a: Failure to check engine instruments after applying takeoff power [[24:138|AFH 6-6]]; coach the takeoff check that power, rpm and engine instruments are normal [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: The rule: before beginning a flight, the PIC must know runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. The AFH says to check the POH/AFM performance charts before going to the airplane and decide if the airplane can take off and climb safely; high density altitude reduces engine and propeller performance, lengthens the takeoff roll and reduces climb [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].
At the run-up, S1 is a review: are today's runway, wind, weight and surface still the ones the numbers were worked for? Teach the size of each effect.

head: Factor
Effect on takeoff distance
Source
rows: Surface not hard and smooth (grass, gravel, mud, snow, water)
Longer ground roll; charts usually assume paved, level, smooth and dry
Takeoff ground roll plus landing ground roll estimates the runway to accelerate and stop

body.p: Takeoffs become more hazardous when the calculated performance approaches the available runway length [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]. Identify a point on the runway where the airplane should be airborne, and reject the takeoff if it is not [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

Teaching the chart work. Learners slip on charts. The AIH describes a learner whose finger drifted to the wrong row and who fixed it by working slowly, using a ruler and double-checking [[25:83|AIH 3-32]]. Let learners find their own errors, then share tactics like these.

check.q: Your learner worked the numbers at 0800 for Runway 27, calm wind, cool air. At the 1300 run-up the ATIS gives a warmer temperature and Runway 9 in use. What must she review before takeoff?
check.a: Rework takeoff distance for the new runway, wind and temperature, since density altitude and wind change the distance [[24:133|AFH 6-1]] [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]], and confirm it against the runway length as 91.103 requires [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]].

chunks.title: The takeoff briefing: say it out loud

body.p: The takeoff briefing is made out loud by the pilot even when no one else is there to listen, and includes a visual check of the correct surface and direction to prevent a wrong-surface departure [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. The AFH sample covers, in order [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]:

bullets: Type of takeoff (normal, short or soft), runway and wind.
Rotation speed from the manufacturer.
Initial turn and initial altitude.
Engine failure below VR: reject, brake, stop ahead.
Engine failure after VR with runway left: lower the pitch, land, brake, stop straight ahead.
Engine failure after VR with no runway left: best glide, no turns before a set altitude, land in the most suitable area.
Turn back only above a stated altitude AGL and MSL; if time permits, fuel, ignition and electrical off.

body.p: The AFH also asks the pilot to consider the preferred direction for any emergency turn, based on the departure path, altitude, wind and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Engine failure during takeoff procedures and significant terrain or obstacles are part of the sample pilot briefing card in AC 91-73B [[7:15|AC 91-73B App 2]].

Teaching it. Have the learner write a briefing for the home runway on the ground, with real landing areas off each end. The AIH suggests leading learners through an event with a low but fixed likelihood, such as an engine failure after takeoff, and having them weigh the outcomes of different responses [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

callout.text: Application: when the learner briefs "land in the most suitable area," ask "Which one?" until she can point to it.

check.q: Your learner's briefing ends with "and if anything goes wrong, I'll handle it." Name three pieces the AFH sample would add.
check.a: Any three of: reject below VR and stop ahead; after VR with runway left, lower the pitch and land ahead; with no runway left, best glide, no turns before a set altitude, land in the most suitable area; a stated turn-back altitude; fuel, ignition and electrical off if time permits [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: Division of attention while conducting before takeoff checks (R1) is a real hazard at the run-up pad. If the parking brake slips, or the toe brakes are not enough for the power applied, the airplane can move forward rapidly and go unnoticed if the pilot looks only inside. A good practice is to split attention from one item inside to a look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

Why learners get it wrong. Switching back and forth between a checklist and the equipment is attention switching, and a task put off for later is easy to forget completely. Interruptions are a significant source of errors: the classic case is a learner who puts down a checklist, handles the interruption, and picks up at a later point, omitting steps [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Fixation on one task is often a sign the task has not been practiced enough in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

head: Risk
Mitigation
Source
rows: Do pre-departure checklists only when stopped, or taxiing straight ahead on a taxiway without complex intersections
Stop completely, or be in a phase of taxi with no risk of an incursion, before continuing checklists
Complete all checklists while stopped; no nonessential chatter during taxi
Application: restart the interrupted section from its beginning, not from where you think you stopped

body.p: Do not be the distraction. Avoid teaching at an inappropriate time, such as discussing takeoff technique while entering the runway; do most of the teaching before contacting the tower or announcing on the CTAF [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. AC 91-73B asks flight schools to have instructors limit cockpit instruction during taxi and to mount panel placards as a reminder [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3]]. Teach the sterile flight deck and model it yourself [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

check.q: Ground calls with a taxi amendment halfway through your learner's magneto check. Afterward she resumes at "carburetor heat." What does the AIH warn about, and what do you teach?
check.a: An interruption can make a learner return to a later point in the checklist and omit steps [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]; teach her to go back and finish the interrupted section from its start.

body.p: Unexpected runway changes by air traffic control (R2) catch learners who have already "flown" the departure in their heads. AC 91-73B names the pitfall: pretaxi planning sets expectations, then ATC gives different instructions. Pilots need to follow the clearance actually received, not the one they expected [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].

head: When ATC changes it
What the learner does
Source
rows: Read back the runway assignment, including left, right or center
Advise ATC; ATC may honor the request when practicable
Assess the intersection; the minimum runway required must fit in the reduced length and declared distances before accepting. Ask for the distance if needed
Say "UNABLE" right away; the final decision to act rests with the pilot
The runway length is reduced by construction; full length is not available

body.p: What a runway change resets: the takeoff performance review (S1), the takeoff briefing and its engine-failure plan, the heading bug, and the wrong-runway check. At airports with close runway thresholds, set the heading bug to the departure runway and make one last scan to confirm the heading matches before adding power [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. A clearance is not authorization to conduct an unsafe operation [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

callout.text: Application: on a dual flight, have the learner brief the likely alternate runway too, so a change becomes a review instead of a scramble. Then teach her to stop and re-brief anyway.

check.q: Holding short of Runway 27, the tower says "Runway 9 now in use, taxi via Alpha." Your learner reaches for the throttle. What does she do first?
check.a: Read back the new runway assignment [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]], follow the clearance actually received, not the expected one [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]], and before departure redo the performance review and takeoff briefing for Runway 9 [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: Taking off immediately behind another aircraft, especially a large heavy transport, risks a wake encounter and loss of control. If it is necessary, avoid the other aircraft's flight path or rotate before the point where it rotated [[24:133|AFH 6-1]]. Vortex strength is greatest when the generating aircraft is heavy, clean and slow [[34:147|AIM 7-4-3]].

head: Departure situation
AIM procedure
Source
rows: Note its rotation point, rotate before it, climb above its climb path until turning clear, avoid headings that cross below and behind it
Watch for larger aircraft operations, especially upwind; avoid headings that cross below a larger aircraft's path
After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go
Vortices settle and drift along the runway; wait at least 2 minutes before your takeoff

body.p: Wind moves the wake. Vortices drift with the wind at about the wind speed; 10 knots moves them about 1,000 feet in a minute [[1:106|PHAK 5-9]]. Near the ground they spread at 2 or 3 knots, and a light crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex in the touchdown zone [[1:107|PHAK 5-10]].

ATC helps but does not fly for you. Whether or not a caution is given, the pilot is expected to adjust to avoid serious wake encounters [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. A small airplane departing from an intersection behind a departing large aircraft gets a 3-minute interval that the pilot may waive on request; behind a B757 it may not be waived [[34:155|AIM 7-4-9c]]. Ask for extra separation as soon as practical on ground control, before taxiing onto the runway [[34:155|AIM 7-4-9f]].

callout.text: Instructor duty: make sure there is enough spacing from landing and departing aircraft before entering any space used for departures and arrivals; it also teaches decision making [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Why do you teach a learner to watch where a departing jet lifts off, not just when it leaves?
check.a: Its wake begins at rotation, so she plans to rotate before that point and climb above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]] [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

chunks.title: Plan for a powerplant failure or other malfunction

body.p: R4 asks you to teach the risk of a potential powerplant failure during takeoff or other malfunction, considering operational factors. Teach each factor by name with what it changes in the plan.

head: Operational factor
What it changes
Source
rows: Glide performance and altitude lost in a gliding turn for this make and model. Some airplanes usually cannot make a turn back, some can under certain conditions.
Where the airplane must be airborne, and whether ground roll plus landing roll fits the runway left.
Soft, grassy, muddy or wet surfaces lengthen the roll and change braking effectiveness.
High density altitude hurts takeoff and climb; wind picks the better turn direction; a night takeoff over water can create a black hole effect.
Trees, buildings and terrain in the departure path limit the landing options and the climb.

body.p: Other malfunctions. A malfunctioning powerplant, inadequate acceleration, a runway incursion or a traffic conflict can each call for a rejected takeoff: power to idle, maximum braking with directional control, and for a fire, mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off, always per the manufacturer's procedure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

After liftoff. At a climb attitude without power the airplane is at or near a stalling angle of attack, so lower the nose immediately, keep it coordinated and glide toward a landing area, preferably straight ahead [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Continuing straight ahead or making a slight turn is usually the lowest risk [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

The FAA's turn-back example shows why: an engine failure at 300 feet AGL, a 4-second reaction and a standard-rate turn through 225 degrees leave the airplane 1,016 feet below the runway [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. A turn back at low altitude is an unacceptable risk for student pilots, low-time and untrained pilots, and airplanes without enough glide [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

A case to teach from. Near maximum gross weight, a pilot took off from a 3,100-foot turf runway with wet grass 3 inches or higher and 100-foot trees at the end; the POH gave data only for a hard surface over a 50-foot obstacle. The airplane descended into the trees [[30:64|RMH C-1]]. The RMH's mitigation: fly the airplane solo to a nearby longer airport and pick up the passengers there [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

check.q: In the RMH turf-runway case, why did the POH not answer the pilot's question, and what mitigation does the RMH suggest?
check.a: The POH had data only for a hard surface over a 50-foot obstacle, not wet grass and 100-foot trees [[30:64|RMH C-1]]; the RMH suggests flying solo to the nearby longer airport to pick up the passengers [[30:65|RMH C-2]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: a run-up lesson

head: Phase
What you do
Source
rows: Give the objective and the why of each item; work the performance numbers with the learner; discuss the hazards of this departure and how to mitigate them
At the pad, stopped, you run the checklist and explain each item and its normal reading, looking outside between items
The learner calls each item and why while you perform it, so misunderstandings are fixed before she is busy with the controls
She runs the check, thinking out loud; you watch her eyes, hands and the brakes, and look outside yourself
Prompt her to say the hazards and mitigations out loud; ask what she would do with a magneto over the limit or a runway change
Ask why an error happened and what would prevent it, without letting her practice the wrong way

body.p: Build it in blocks. Before asking a learner to combine tasks, make sure each one can be done reasonably well alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Teach reading the gauges on the ground first, then the full check, then the full check with ATC calls, traffic and a runway change.

Teach the order of attention. Most of your teaching belongs at the pad, before contacting the tower [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Once the learner is cleared onto the runway, your words are short and only about safety.

callout.text: On the CFI practical test the Skills elements are "demonstrates and simultaneously explains" (ACS AI.V.F). Practice narrating a full run-up from the right seat: what you check, the normal reading and why it matters.

check.q: Your learner fixates on the checklist card and misses an airplane taxiing behind her. What does the AIH say fixation usually tells you, and how do you adjust the lesson?
check.a: Fixation is often a sign the task has not had enough practice in isolation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]; practice the run-up items on their own until they are easy, then add the outside scan and radio work.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Yoke and rudder moved part of the way
Full deflection in all directions; partial is not acceptable [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
High power on a cold engine
Run-up power right after a short taxi
Verify oil temperature is in range first [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Airplane creeping forward at run-up power
One item inside, one look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Gravel, debris, or something behind the tail
Move to a firm, clean spot clear of aircraft and the taxiway [[24:58|AFH 2-21]]
Return to the interrupted step; interruptions omit steps [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]
Fast words, no look at the gauge
Slow down and tie each word to a look or touch [[25:79|AIH 3-28]]
Drop over the limit, or no drop, called good
Short taxi, quick check, gyros barely spun up
Give gyros time; a hasty run-up makes an IMC departure unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]
Cannot say the takeoff distance or lift-off point
Review the charts before going to the airplane [[24:138|AFH 6-6]] [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]
Taxis toward the planned runway after a change
Follow the clearance received; re-brief [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]]
Rolling right behind a larger aircraft
No plan for its rotation point
Rotate before its rotation point or wait [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
No reject point, no landing area, a turn back assumed
Brief out loud with the AFH elements [[24:59|AFH 2-22]] [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]

callout.text: Errors are a resource: ask the learner why it happened and what would prevent it, but do not let her keep practicing the wrong way [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: During your learner's run-up the airplane creeps forward a few feet and she does not notice. What allowed it, and what habit fixes it?
check.a: A slipping parking brake or too little toe brake for the power, unnoticed because her attention was only inside; split attention, one item inside and a look outside [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

f1.alt: Photograph of a small high-wing airplane taxiing on a grass-edged taxiway directly in front of a much larger four-engine jet airliner, showing how close the two are on the ground.

f3.caption: Figure 11-19. Effect of wind on takeoff and landing. (PHAK 11-15)
f3.alt: Graph of the ratio of wind velocity to takeoff or landing speed against percent change in distance. A red reference line rises steeply for tailwind, with a dashed example near 10 percent tailwind giving about a 25 percent increase. A green curve for headwind shows the percent decrease.

f4.alt: A jet seen from behind with two vortices sinking to the ground. With a 3-knot wind from the right, the left vortex moves away at 6 knots (3 plus 3) and the right, upwind vortex stays nearly in place at 0 (3 minus 3).

scenario.title: A busy run-up pad on a warm afternoon
scenario.setup: You are teaching a pre-solo learner in the school's carbureted, fixed-pitch trainer at a towered airport on a warm, humid afternoon. She stops for the run-up on a gravel patch, nose downwind, behind a parked twin. During the magneto check, Ground calls: "Runway 9 now in use, taxi to Runway 9 at Charlie, intersection departure." A business jet has just made a touch-and-go on Runway 9 with a light quartering wind. When she pulls carburetor heat, the rpm drops and then slowly rises.

questions.q: Before she adds any power, what do you have her fix about where she stopped?
questions.a: Move to a firm spot free of debris, clear of other aircraft, with nothing behind that the blast could damage, headed as nearly into the wind as possible, then roll forward to align the nosewheel [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

questions.q: What does the carburetor heat reading tell you, and what do you teach?
questions.a: In a fixed-pitch airplane, a drop followed by a gradual rise means ice was present and is melting [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Leave the heat on until the ice is gone, and treat the conditions as conducive to carburetor icing [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: Ground's call came halfway through the magneto check. How does she pick the checklist back up?
questions.a: Interruptions make learners resume at a later point and omit steps [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Application: she returns to the start of the magneto check and finishes it before moving on.

questions.q: What must she do before accepting the Charlie intersection on Runway 9?
questions.a: Read back the runway [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7b]], ask the distance from Charlie if needed [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]], confirm the required runway fits the reduced length [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]], and re-brief the takeoff and engine-failure plan for the new runway [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. If it does not fit, she says "unable" [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

questions.q: A business jet just did a touch-and-go on Runway 9. As her instructor, how do you handle the wake risk before she rolls?
questions.a: Vortices settle and move along the runway, especially in a light quartering wind, so wait at least 2 minutes before the takeoff [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. As instructor you make sure the spacing is there before entering the runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

questions.q: When do you teach during all this, and when do you stay quiet?
questions.a: Teach at the pad before contacting the tower; do not teach technique while she enters the runway [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Keep instruction during taxi to a minimum [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3]] and model a sterile flight deck [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to review takeoff performance (AI.V.F.S1). There is no numeric tolerance. Expect to confirm the takeoff distance, runway available, wind, surface and lift-off point for this departure, and explain how you teach a learner to check them.
skills.practice: Before every flight, work the POH charts for the runway in use and say the accelerate-stop estimate out loud [[24:146|AFH 6-14]]. Rework them at the run-up whenever the runway or wind changes [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to complete the appropriate checklist(s) (AI.V.F.S2). No numeric tolerance: use the airplane's AFM/POH before-takeoff checklist, give the reason for each item as you do it, and give the takeoff briefing out loud.
skills.practice: Run the checklist from the right seat while explaining each item and its normal reading [[24:58|AFH 2-21]] [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], and practice the AFH briefing until it is short and natural.

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to position the airplane appropriately considering wind direction and the presence of any aircraft, vessels, or buildings as applicable (AI.V.F.S3). No numeric tolerance: pick a firm, clean spot clear of aircraft and the taxiway, nothing behind, nose into the wind, nosewheel aligned.
skills.practice: At every run-up, say out loud what is behind the tail and where the wind is from before adding power [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to divide attention inside and outside the flight deck (AI.V.F.S4). No numeric tolerance: look outside between items, keep the brakes and the airplane's position in mind, and explain how you teach it.
skills.practice: Use the one-item-inside, one-look-outside rhythm on every run-up [[24:58|AFH 2-21]], and run checklists only when stopped [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(a)]].

skills.do: The ACS says you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to verify that engine parameters and airplane configuration are suitable (AI.V.F.S5). No numeric tolerance: show each reading against its POH limit, the configuration for the takeoff, and the takeoff checks as power comes up.
skills.practice: Memorize your trainer's POH limits and say the normal reading and the bad one for each check [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]] [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]; call the six takeoff checks on every roll [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

quiz.q: Why are small chips in a propeller's leading edge dangerous?
options: They only affect paint and finish
They form stress risers that can lead to cracks and blade failure
They make the run-up noisier but are harmless
They reduce fuel flow to the engine
quiz.why: Small chips form stress risers or high stress concentrations that may lead to cracks and possible blade failure [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

quiz.q: After positioning for the run-up, what does the AFH say to do before starting the check?
options: Set the parking brake and add full power
Roll forward slightly so the nosewheel or tailwheel is aligned
Turn the airplane 90 degrees to the wind
Shut down and restart the engine
quiz.why: Let the airplane roll forward slightly to align the nosewheel or tailwheel with the longitudinal axis [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

quiz.q: Why can a long ground run hurt a tightly cowled air-cooled engine?
options: Oil temperature drops too low
Cylinders can overheat before oil temperature shows it
The magnetos lose their charge
The propeller governor freezes
quiz.why: Prolonged ground operations may cause cylinder overheating long before oil temperature rises [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

quiz.q: Aligned on the runway with an accurate compass, how closely should the heading indicator match the runway direction?
options: Within 5 degrees
Within 15 degrees
Within 30 degrees
It need not match
quiz.why: The heading indicator should show the known runway direction within 5 degrees [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].

quiz.q: What danger does the AIH name in attention switching during a checklist?
options: The pilot reads too slowly
A deferred task can be forgotten completely
The checklist becomes too short
The pilot looks outside too often
quiz.why: A task postponed for later is easy to forget completely [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

quiz.q: AC 91-73B suggests placards on the panels of school airplanes to remind instructors to:
options: Check fuel quantity
Limit cockpit instruction during critical phases, particularly taxi
Turn on the landing light
Read back hold short instructions
quiz.why: Instructors should limit cockpit instruction during critical phases, particularly taxiing, with placards as a reminder [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3]].

quiz.q: Before accepting an intersection takeoff, what must be true?
options: The tower must say it is long enough
The minimum runway required fits within the reduced runway length and declared distances
The intersection must be within 500 feet of the threshold
The wind must be calm
quiz.why: The minimum runway required for takeoff must fall within the reduced runway length and reduced declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]].

quiz.q: A small airplane departing from an intersection behind a departing large aircraft (not a B757) is held for 3 minutes. Can the pilot waive it?
options: No, never
Yes, on specific pilot request
Only at night
Only if the tower suggests it
quiz.why: This 3-minute interval may be waived upon specific pilot request [[34:155|AIM 7-4-9c]].

quiz.q: According to the RMH, when do takeoffs become more hazardous?
options: When the calculated performance approaches the available runway length
Only above 5,000 feet elevation
Only on paved runways
Only with passengers aboard
quiz.why: Takeoffs and landings become more hazardous when the calculated performance approaches the available runway length [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

quiz.q: For whom does the AFH call a low-altitude turn back an unacceptable risk?
options: Only airline pilots
Student pilots, low-time and untrained pilots, and airplanes with too little glide
Only pilots of retractable-gear airplanes
Nobody; it is always the best choice
quiz.why: A turn back at low altitude is an unacceptable risk for student, low-time, untrained or non-proficient pilots and for airplanes with insufficient glide performance [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner switches to RIGHT and the engine quits. She switches back to BOTH, it runs smoothly, and she says, "Must have been a glitch." What is the correct call?
options: Fly; it runs on BOTH
Do not fly until the problem is corrected
Fly, but only in the pattern
Lean the mixture and try again until it passes
final_quiz.why: If the engine stops running on one magneto or the drop exceeds the limit, do not fly until the problem is corrected [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

final_quiz.q: On the first flight after an annual, the run-up is slightly rough on one magneto but within the POH limit. Which RMH point should shape your decision?
options: Annuals guarantee airworthiness
Difficulty with a run-up or an engine issue after maintenance may be a significant hazard
Roughness within limits is never a concern
Only the mechanic decides
final_quiz.why: The RMH lists difficulty with an engine run-up or an engine issue after maintenance as a possible significant hazard [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]; the AIH's throttle rod-end story shows why [[25:5|AIH 1-1]].

final_quiz.q: A learner who handles each run-up item well alone starts missing traffic once you add ATC calls. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Add more tasks until it clicks
Make sure each task can be done reasonably well in isolation before combining them
Skip the run-up on busy days
Do the radio work for her permanently
final_quiz.why: Before learners perform several tasks at once, make sure each can be done reasonably well in isolation; fixation often signals too little practice alone [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

final_quiz.q: ATC switches you from Runway 27 to Runway 9. Your briefing planned emergency turns to the left toward an open field. What does the AFH say should decide the new plan?
options: Keep the same turn direction
The departure path, altitude, wind and terrain for Runway 9
Always turn right after a runway change
Whatever the tower suggests
final_quiz.why: The preferred direction for emergency turns is based on the departure path, altitude, wind conditions and terrain [[24:133|AFH 6-1]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH requires 1,800 feet for today's takeoff. Tower offers an intersection departure with 1,750 feet available. Best response?
options: Accept; ATC knows the length
Decline and request full length
Accept and use a short-field technique
Accept and rotate early
final_quiz.why: The minimum runway required must fit within the reduced length [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]]; if you prefer the full length you inform ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]], and "unable" is fine when you cannot comply safely [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

final_quiz.q: Tower says "N123, Runway 9, line up and wait." Your learner replies "Roger." What should she have said?
options: Wilco
Her call sign and the runway designator in a full readback
Nothing; LUAW needs no reply
Ready for takeoff
final_quiz.why: Include the complete call sign and runway designator when reading back a clearance to taxi to LUAW, and avoid "Roger" or "Wilco" [[7:8|AC 91-73B 7f(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is in a small airplane at an intersection behind a departing B757 and asks for a waiver of the 3-minute hold. What happens?
options: ATC grants it on request
This interval may not be waived
ATC must reduce it to 1 minute
She must depart from the threshold instead
final_quiz.why: Behind a departing B757 from an intersection, the 3-minute interval may not be waived [[34:155|AIM 7-4-9c]].

final_quiz.q: A heavy jet departs from the same threshold you will use. Under the AIM, what interval does ATC apply, and may it be waived?
options: 1 minute, waivable
2 minutes or radar separation, not reduced or waived
No interval for VFR
5 minutes, waivable
final_quiz.why: Two minutes or the appropriate radar separation behind a heavy, and controllers may not reduce or waive these intervals [[34:154|AIM 7-4-9b]].

final_quiz.q: In the RMH turf-runway accident, what did the POH not provide?
options: Takeoff data for a hard surface
Takeoff data for wet grass or a 100-foot obstacle
The airplane's gross weight
The rotation speed
final_quiz.why: The POH gave about 1,700 feet for a hard surface over a 50-foot obstacle, but no data for a wet-grass turf runway or a 100-foot obstacle [[30:64|RMH C-1]].

final_quiz.q: An experienced private pilot asks you to train the turn back after an engine failure. Which AFH guidance fits?
options: Practice at pattern altitude over the runway
Practice turns both ways at a safe altitude in the make and model, and expect the high end of the altitude loss
Use a standard-rate turn to save altitude
Do not practice; just brief it
final_quiz.why: Practice turns in both directions at a safe altitude after a simulated failure from a climb, aim for consistent altitude loss, and expect the high end of the range in a real event [[24:356|AFH 18-7]].

final_quiz.q: Smoke comes from the cowling during the takeoff roll. After power to idle and maximum braking with directional control, what does the AFH add for a fire?
options: Carburetor heat on
Mixture to idle cutoff and magnetos off
Flaps full down
Cycle the propeller
final_quiz.why: If it is necessary to shut down the engine due to fire, bring the mixture to idle cutoff and turn the magnetos off, following the manufacturer's procedure [[24:146|AFH 6-14]].

final_quiz.q: Which items does AC 91-73B want completed before initial taxi?
options: None; do everything at the run-up
As many as possible, such as flaps, trim and GPS inputs
Only the passenger briefing
Only the takeoff briefing
final_quiz.why: Complete as many checklist items as possible, such as flaps, trim and GPS navigation inputs, before initial taxi [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2)(g)]].

final_quiz.q: Under the AIH, what is the main purpose of the 5P check just before takeoff?
options: To file a flight plan
A reasoned go/no-go decision based on all available information
To check the weather at the destination only
To brief passengers on exits
final_quiz.why: Correctly applied before takeoff, the 5P check helps make a reasoned go/no-go decision [[25:20|AIH 1-16]].

takeaways: Teach the why: every before-takeoff item has a reason, a normal reading and a bad one.
A failed check stops the flight: engine quits on a magneto or the drop is over the limit, do not fly.
The AFM/POH sets the limits and the order; the manufacturer's recommendations take precedence.
Run up on a firm, clean spot, nose into the wind, nothing behind, nosewheel aligned.
One item inside, one look outside; checklists only when stopped; restart after an interruption.
A runway change resets the performance review, the briefing and the heading bug; follow the clearance you got.
Rotate before a larger aircraft's rotation point, and plan straight ahead for an engine failure at low altitude.
cfi_notes: Sources differ on vacuum: the AFH gives typically 4.8 to 5.2 "Hg at 2,000 rpm [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], the PHAK usually 4.5 to 5.5 "Hg [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Both defer to the manufacturer; teach the POH number.

The AFH sample briefing says "no turns will be made prior to" an altitude and "I will only consider turning back if I have reached at least __ feet AGL" [[24:59|AFH 2-22]], but no source gives a number. That number comes from training in the make and model at a safe altitude [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]; do not give a learner a rule-of-thumb altitude from memory.
The FAA turn-back example uses a standard-rate turn to show why a standard-rate turn fails [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]; make sure learners do not take it as the technique.
The PHAK says no magneto drop is not normal [[1:176|PHAK 7-16]]. Learners often think it is the best result; ask them about it on the ground before they see it.

Teaching at the run-up is good; teaching on the runway is not. Do the talking at the pad and before contacting the tower [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and keep instruction during taxi to a minimum [[7:17|AC 91-73B App 3]].
For the CFI test, the S elements have no numeric tolerances; the examiner judges whether you demonstrate and explain at the same time, so rehearse narrating from the right seat.
Seaplane items in S3 (vessels) do not apply to ASEL; a one-line mention is enough.
The PHAK wake drift figure (10 knots of wind moves vortices about 1,000 feet a minute) is approximate [[1:106|PHAK 5-9]]; use it to teach the idea, not to time a departure to the second.
gaps: No source gives the magneto drop limit, the allowed difference between magnetos, run-up rpm, minimum oil temperature or propeller-cycle rpm for a specific airplane; use the AFM/POH.
The sources give no specific turn-back altitude; it must be found by training in the make and model with an authorized instructor.
No source gives a minimum distance from other aircraft or buildings for the run-up; the AFH says only clear of them with nothing behind that could be damaged.
The sources do not give one standard order for the run-up; the AFH list is a minimum and the AFM/POH order governs.
No source gives takeoff data for surfaces or obstacles the POH does not cover, as the RMH turf case shows; a CFI must teach conservative margins and alternatives.

activities.title: What is the reading telling you?
activities.intro: Tap a reading, then what it means.

pairs.l: Fixed pitch, carburetor heat on: rpm drops, then slowly rises
pairs.r: Carburetor ice was there and is melting

pairs.l: Altimeter 90 feet off field elevation with the current setting
Horizon bar tips more than 5 degrees in taxi turns
Rough at run-up power, full rich, high-elevation airport
pairs.r: Mixture too rich; lean per the POH

activities.why: Ammeter [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]; carburetor heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]; altimeter [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]; attitude indicator [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]; mixture [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

activities.title: From taxiway to takeoff roll
activities.intro: Put the steps in the order the AFH describes them, then tap Check.
steps: Pick a firm spot free of debris, clear of aircraft and the taxiway, nothing behind
Head as nearly into the wind as possible
Roll forward slightly to align the nosewheel
Verify oil temperature is in range before high power
Run the systems checks per the AFM/POH, looking outside between items
Set instruments and avionics for the departure
Give the takeoff briefing out loud
On the runway, check numbers against the compass and heading indicator, then run the takeoff checks as power comes up

activities.title: Run-up numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Zero-wind takeoff distance is 1,100 feet. Today you will have a tailwind that is 10 percent of your takeoff speed. About how far, in feet?
items.why: A 10 percent tailwind increases takeoff distance about 21 percent: 1,100 x 1.21 = 1,331 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: POH takeoff ground roll is 1,050 feet and landing ground roll is 640 feet. The intersection you are offered leaves 2,000 feet. How many feet of margin beyond the accelerate-stop estimate?
Your learner computed 1,100 feet with no wind. The ATIS now gives a headwind of about 10 percent of her lift-off speed. About what distance should she expect, in feet?
items.why: A headwind of 10 percent of takeoff airspeed reduces takeoff distance about 19 percent: 1,100 x 0.81 = 891 ft [[1:271|PHAK 11-15]].

items.q: Field elevation is 1,135 feet. With the current altimeter setting, the altimeter reads 1,215 feet. How many feet off is it?
items.why: 1,215 - 1,135 = 80 ft, more than 75 ft, so accuracy is questionable [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

items.q: A 10-knot wind moves wake vortices about 1,000 feet per minute. About how far do they drift in 90 seconds?
items.why: 1,000 ft per minute x 1.5 minutes = 1,500 ft [[1:106|PHAK 5-9]].

activities.title: True or false: runway changes
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If you prefer the full runway length to an offered intersection, you are expected to tell ATC.
cards.why: True. If for any reason a pilot prefers a different intersection or the full length, the pilot informs ATC [[33:252|AIM 4-3-10a]].

cards.s: Once ATC assigns a runway, a pilot may not ask for a different one.
cards.why: False. A pilot who prefers a different runway is expected to advise ATC, and ATC may honor it [[33:245|AIM 4-3-6c]].

cards.s: Telling a controller "unable" is appropriate when you cannot safely comply.
cards.why: True. Inform ATC immediately using the word UNABLE [[1:367|PHAK 14-33]].

cards.s: On request, controllers give the distance from an intersection to the end of each declared distance.
cards.why: False. They give the measured distance to the runway end, rounded down to the nearest 50 feet, but not to the declared distances [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10c]].

cards.s: Pretaxi planning can lead a pilot to follow the instructions expected instead of those received.
cards.why: True. That is the CAUTION in AC 91-73B [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]].

cards.s: The initial readback of a departure clearance should include the runway assignment, with left, right or center if applicable.

activities.title: Which R4 factor is it?
activities.intro: Tap a hazard, then the operational factor it belongs to.

items.t: Not enough glide to return to the field
Altitude lost in a gliding 180 degree turn in this make and model
Calculated takeoff distance close to the runway available
Wet grass 3 inches tall on a turf runway
Mud or standing water slowing acceleration
High temperature at a high-elevation airport
Night takeoff over a large body of water
Buildings in the departure path at an urban airport

activities.title: Read the turn-back figure
activities.intro: Drag each label to the part of the FAA turn-back example it names.

pins.label: Sideways distance after the first 180 degrees
Height below runway level at the end of the turn

activities.title: Teaching a run-up, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are giving a learner her fourth lesson in the school's fixed-pitch trainer at a towered airport. Decide what you do as the instructor at each step.

steps.s: On the ramp she says, "Let's just follow the checklist today; the reasons can wait."
options: Agree; reasons come later
Brief the why of the items and today's departure hazards before you go
Skip the run-up to save time
Do the whole run-up yourself
steps.why: Discuss hazards and risk mitigation in detail during preflight [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and teach understanding, which helps her handle variations later [[25:61|AIH 3-10]].

steps.s: The only open run-up spot is a gravel patch with a parked airplane right behind it.
options: Use it; it is only for a minute
Wait for, or move to, a firm spot with nothing behind
Do the run-up on the taxiway
Skip the magneto check
steps.why: Use a firm spot free of debris, clear of other aircraft and the taxiway, with nothing behind that the blast could damage [[24:58|AFH 2-21]].

steps.s: The right magneto drop is over the POH limit. She says, "Probably plugs. It runs fine on BOTH."
options: Go; BOTH is what you fly on
Do not fly; taxi back and write it up
Try it ten more times until it passes
Fly the pattern only
steps.why: If the drop exceeds the allowable limit, do not fly until the problem is corrected [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].

steps.s: Another day: holding short, Tower changes her runway and offers an intersection she has not planned.
options: Accept and go
Read back, then check the length and re-brief before accepting
Refuse any change
Ask you to decide
steps.why: Follow the clearance actually received [[7:4|AC 91-73B 7b(2) CAUTION]], assess the intersection [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10b]] and re-brief for the new runway [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

steps.s: A large jet has just departed from the runway end. Tower tells her intersection departure, "Hold for wake turbulence." She wants to request a waiver.
options: Request the waiver; it saves 3 minutes
Wait out the interval and use the time to review the plan
Taxi onto the runway and wait there
Depart from a different intersection without asking
steps.why: The 3-minute interval behind a departing large aircraft can be waived, but then the pilot takes on wake separation [[33:253|AIM 4-3-10f]]; you ensure sufficient spacing before entering the departure area [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
